New

  • Lavalink template: an audio server for Discord music bots. It starts with no plugins and no domain. Its application.yml is kept in a volume, so you can add plugins and change settings on the Files page, then restart. A Java options field sets the memory it may use.
  • Templates can start without a domain. You can still add one on Domains & ports, where the template's port is already filled in.

Fixed

  • A running service is no longer shown as Crashed when a status report from its server comes back empty. Serve now checks the containers directly before it marks a service as crashed.

Polished

  • The IP address field of a server is hidden until you press the eye button, so it stays private on a shared screen or in a recording. Password managers do not offer to save it.

Security

  • Compose files that hide a value behind a YAML tag such as !!binary are refused. A member of any organization could use one to slip host access (the host's network, its process namespace, mounts of / or the Docker socket) past the check, on servers their organization deploys to. Builds on the host's network, privileged builds and network drivers other than bridge are refused too. Upgrading is recommended for every instance with more than one organization.
  • The database connection API no longer shows the password inside the pooler and read replica URLs to tokens without the permission to see secrets.
  • Log drain addresses, which can hold API keys, are no longer sent to members who do not manage integrations. Members limited to some projects cannot change log drains or notification channels, which cover every project. The log drain test connects only to a public address.
  • Reading a shared server's custom proxy files, deploying uploaded files to an app built from Git, copying data when cloning an environment, changing deploy approval and seeing a tag's deploy hook each need the right permission now.
  • The volume download only offers the container's volumes and mounts.
  • The request log no longer keeps tokens that were in the Referer's query string.
  • Next.js 16.3.8.

New

  • Files: browse, upload, download, edit, rename and delete files on a server's disk or inside a service's container, from the sidebar or a Files tab on servers and services. Pick several items to download them as one .tar.gz or delete them, right-click for a row's actions, edit text files in the code editor and go full screen.
  • The CLI gets serve upload, serve download and serve ls, for servers (hetzner:/srv/) and services (-s web :/app/). A folder uploads as one archive, and serve download -x unpacks a folder.
  • Closest server: an app that runs on several servers can get one Cloudflare Tunnel with a connector on each of them, so every visitor reaches the nearest server and another one when a server is down. Turning it off puts each domain back the way it was before.
  • Terminal in the sidebar: pick a server or a service, and switch between them from the breadcrumb.
  • Full screen for logs, the console and the server terminal.
  • Your own certificate can be used on any server of an app; Serve copies it there.
  • On the canvas, an app that runs on several servers shows a card on each of them. A button hides the variable names on the lines.

Fixed

  • Turning Closest server off no longer leaves visitors without an answer for a few minutes, and ending it by removing or moving the last domain turns load balancing back on.
  • A failed restore's safety backup is never removed by retention, the newest backup that passed its restore test is always kept, and backups of some databases no longer push out the full ones. Two backups started in the same second no longer share a file.
  • Removing a server with its data kept keeps its backup files.
  • Restoring an instance backup saves the current database first, restores in one transaction and puts it back if anything fails.
  • Docker cleanup keeps images that were built on the machine.
  • The private network makes link containers only for services the server's apps use, and keeps them while running containers may still use them.

Polished

  • Domains & ports has a sidebar of sections, and the add domain dialog is shorter: the server choice folds away, HTTPS is one choice, the Cloudflare record says Proxied or DNS only.
  • Recent deploys show a green light for a deploy that worked, red for one that failed and grey for a cancelled one.
  • Units beside a field, such as "/ min", stay on one line.

New

  • Volumes on the canvas. Every card shows its volumes under it, with a short name and its size, like Railway. Sizes update every minute; hover shows the full volume name and where it is mounted.
  • Data kept from deleted services. Delete a database, app or compose stack and keep its data, and a dashed card stays in its project: "From deleted <name>", with its size. Start a database on it brings a database back on that data, and Delete data removes it for good (type its name and your password). Folders on the server and volumes made outside Serve are only forgotten, never deleted. Kept data also shows in the grid and list views.
  • Read replicas can be started again. A stopped replica has a Start button. Starting or restarting the database starts its replicas on every server, and a redeploy starts each replica on its own, so one server that does not answer no longer keeps the others down.
  • The API lists and deletes kept data: GET /environments/{id}/kept-data, DELETE /kept-data/{kind}/{id}.

Fixed

  • A stopped read replica marked its whole database as down. Only the database itself, or its pooler, does now.

Serve 0.5.0 sums up everything since 0.4.0: one app on many servers, backups you can trust, public status pages, a login wall for any app, and an API and CLI that cover the whole dashboard.

Highlights since 0.4.0

One app, many servers

  • Load balancing across servers. Tick extra servers, turn on load balancing, deploy. Visitors reach replicas on every server through the private network. DNS only points at the main server; the others need no records and no open ports.
  • Health checked every 5 seconds. A replica that stops answering gets no visitors until it is back. Each server switches to a new version only once its replicas are healthy.
  • Pick how visitors are spread: round robin, least busy (good for uploads, streams and AI calls), sticky sessions, or main server first with failover to the others in about 10 seconds.
  • Switch the main server without a redeploy. Domains, certificates and load balancing move over, and Serve moves the Cloudflare DNS records and tunnel domains it made. If the main server dies, make another one main and the app is back.
  • Build once, run anywhere. A built app runs on several servers, or uses a build server, without a registry: Serve copies the image.

Backups you can trust

  • Every restore is safe. Serve backs up everything first, and puts it back at once when a restore fails.
  • Backup tests. Serve restores a backup into a throwaway database, by hand or every day, and tells you when one fails.
  • Encrypted with your own passphrase, in a format openssl opens without Serve. Every backup has a checksum that is checked before it is restored.
  • Several buckets, with the next one used when one is down. Backups before each deploy, users and passwords included if you want, MySQL, MariaDB and ClickHouse compressed.
  • Import any dump from a file, a URL or a bucket, with the restore window showing the upload's progress. Compose stacks back up and import their databases, volumes and folders.
  • Compose stacks can roll back to exactly the files and images a past deployment ran.

Status pages

  • A public status page in minutes. Components follow your uptime checks, incidents and maintenance with updates, postmortems, and outages that show up on their own.
  • Your design and your domain: four looks, logos, colors, fonts, any language, a response time chart, password or draft visibility, and your own domain through the server's IP or a Cloudflare Tunnel. Serve creates the DNS record when Cloudflare manages it.
  • Subscribers follow by email, Slack, Discord, webhook or RSS, and pick the components they care about. A badge, a website widget and JSON come with every page, and CI can post incidents through the API.

A login wall for any app

  • Only my team puts a sign-in in front of any app: admin panels, internal tools, staging sites. Members with access to the project get in.
  • Guest logins let people without a Serve account in, with an email and password set per app. Works with nginx, Caddy and Traefik.

See every request

  • Request log: each request through the proxy, with which server and replica answered, live in Metrics and Logs, with status and path filters.

Domains, previews and sign-in

  • Edit a domain like you add one: its name, route or redirect, port, tunnel or IP, HTTPS and certificate, and its Cloudflare record and proxy.
  • Pull request previews comment on GitHub, GitLab, Gitea/Forgejo and Bitbucket.
  • Sign in with Microsoft, GitLab and Bitbucket, or your company's login with presets for Keycloak, Authentik, Okta, Auth0, Zitadel, Pocket ID and more.
  • Deleting servers, services and projects asks for your password.

API and CLI for everything

  • 305 API operations cover what the dashboard does, from status pages and database add-ons to deploy rules, Cloudflare and Git credentials. The CLI gained replicas, database settings, tokens, the request log, compose backups, proxy actions and status page incidents.

Fixed in 0.5.0

  • A status page served with a Cloudflare Origin certificate got a DNS only record, and browsers refused the certificate. Serve now makes its record with Cloudflare's proxy on.
  • Check DNS says when a status page reaches the server directly with a Cloudflare Origin certificate, and Turn on Cloudflare proxy fixes the record Serve made.
  • Automatic picks a certificate browsers trust before a Cloudflare Origin one, and the status page picker says when a certificate is a Cloudflare Origin one.

Every release in between, with all its fixes: changelog.

New

  • Edit a domain like you add one: its name, route or redirect, port, Cloudflare Tunnel or server IP, HTTPS and certificate, and its Cloudflare DNS record and proxy.
  • Compose stacks can roll back. Each deployment records its compose file, commit and images, and a rollback runs exactly those. Deployments made before this release cannot roll back.
  • Status pages: Serve creates the A record of their domain when a connected Cloudflare account manages it, and removes it with the page. A Create A record button fixes a missing one.
  • Preview comments on GitLab, Gitea/Forgejo and Bitbucket, as on GitHub.
  • ClickHouse has a Users tab: add logins, change passwords and access, delete them.
  • The API covers what the dashboard does: status pages, database pooler and public access, main database, deploy rules and approvals, HTTP options, compose storage, request log settings, preview databases, server variables, OS updates, Cloudflare, Git credentials, repository webhooks and tailnets.
  • The CLI gained database replicas, settings, public port and domain, preview and replica variables, tokens create, the request log, compose backups, proxy actions, trusted proxies, status page incidents and branch clean-up SQL.

Fixed

  • Promoting a read replica could leave the old database running, so two writable copies. It now stops unless the old one is confirmed gone.
  • ClickHouse in compose stacks was never offered for backups. It is now, and every one of its databases is backed up, not only default.
  • A renewed certificate that a proxy could not load passed as loaded. It is now shown on the certificate and alerted.
  • Removing a domain, service or project hid DNS records, replicas and certificates it could not remove. You now get a warning, and the activity log keeps it.
  • Anyone who could comment on a pull request could get Serve to edit their comment instead of its own. Existing GitHub preview comments get one new comment on the next deploy.
  • The primary domain could be turned into a redirect.
  • Restore errors from ClickHouse and MongoDB showed a useless line instead of the reason.
  • API paths were decoded more than once, so a compose backup key with / or % needed odd encoding. Encode once now.

Polished

  • Every site serves the best certificate covering its name: its own before a wildcard, then the one valid longest. The status page picker says which one Automatic uses.
  • A failed preview DNS record is reported instead of a link that does not work.
  • Over 80 new tests for the job queue, backups, certificates, nginx sites, variables and shell quoting.

Fixed

  • A backup, restore or import that ran past its time limit kept running in the background while a new restore could start on the same database. Its commands are stopped now, and the next one waits until they have.
  • Choosing the main database in Settings → Credentials was only shown to admins; it needs the same permission as on the Connect card.

Breaking

  • A restore now leaves the database exactly as the backup is. Restoring a whole backup removes every database on the server first (not branches, not the engine's own), then brings back the backup's databases and tables under their own names. Restore only some databases by unticking the others.

New

  • A backup of everything is taken before every restore, and put back at once when the restore fails, for the databases it had changed. Tick Keep a backup of the current database to keep it afterwards.
  • Backups have their own pages: Backups, Import backup and Auto backup.
  • Import backup brings a file in first and opens the restore window with the upload's progress. Cancel deletes the file. A dump made for another engine is refused before anything changes.
  • Backups can be encrypted with your own passphrase, in a format openssl opens without Serve.
  • Backups can include the server's users and passwords (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB).
  • Backup tests restore a backup into a throwaway database, by hand or every day, and tell you when one fails.
  • Backups can go to several buckets; when one is down the next one is used.
  • Apps can back up their databases before each deploy.
  • Back up now can store a backup elsewhere, with users or without encryption, for that backup only.
  • MySQL, MariaDB and ClickHouse backups are compressed, and every backup has a checksum that is checked before it is restored.
  • ClickHouse in compose stacks, and compose stacks can import backups into their databases, volumes and folders.
  • The connection URL can name any database of the server, from the Connect card or Settings → Credentials. A restore whose backup lacks the main database makes its first database the main one.
  • The Connect card shows the pooled and read replica connection URLs while they are on.
  • The API and CLI cover all of it: restore choices, backup tests, downloads, uploads and backup settings.

Fixed

  • MySQL row counts in the data explorer were 0 after a restore.
  • A PostgreSQL dump made without --clean failed on tables that already existed.
  • A dump with one database went into the main database whatever its name; it keeps its name now.
  • Compose database passwords were visible on the server's process list during backups.
  • Instance backup downloads failed after an S3 change.

Polished

  • Auto backup is one card with its settings side by side, and only shows them while it is on.
  • Imported files keep their own name, and their safety backup is listed under them.
  • From bucket says where to add S3 storage when there is none.
  • Restore errors show the database's own reason.

Fixed

  • The password field in confirmation dialogs fills in from the password manager again. The type-to-confirm field above it stays empty.

New

  • Guest logins on the login wall: people without a Serve account sign in with an email and password set per app.
  • Access control is now in a service's Settings as well as in Domains.

Fixed

  • Confirmation dialogs no longer get saved credentials filled in by the browser.

Polished

  • Access control is split into three cards: HTTP Basic Auth, Login wall and IP rules. Basic Auth has its switch in the card header.
  • Guests are added from a small form; saved guests show without a password field.
  • A removed guest, or one with a new password, is signed out within 30 seconds. Sign-in attempts are limited to 10 per 15 minutes.
  • The login wall page is a single card with a short note, without the sign-in side panel.
  • The README overview banner is 16:9.

New

  • A login wall for any app: turn on "Only my team" in an app's Domains → Access control to put a sign-in in front of it, good for admin panels, internal tools and staging sites.
  • Visitors sign in to Serve first. Members who can open the app's project get in; everyone else sees "No access".
  • The app's domain keeps the sign-in for 7 days. Signing out of Serve, or removing a member, closes the wall within 30 seconds.
  • Serve's own uptime checks still reach the app.
  • Works with nginx, Caddy and Traefik, on the dashboard's server and on other servers.
  • The app's Overview and Domains pages show "Team only" when it is on.
  • Give the dashboard its own domain first, since visitors sign in there.

Polished

  • The service Details card shows only what differs from the defaults.
  • The sidebar logo is as tall as the name and version next to it.

New

  • Visitors can follow a status page. A page's new Subscribers tab lets you choose which ways it offers: Email (the address is confirmed with a link first, and every email has a one-click unsubscribe), Slack and Discord (visitors paste a channel webhook, and Serve sends a test message before saving it), Webhook (any https URL gets a JSON message for each post; addresses in private networks are refused), and RSS as before.
  • Subscribers can pick the components they care about. They hear about new incidents, updates, planned maintenance, and when a maintenance window starts and ends. A page can also send the outages its uptime checks find.
  • Notification messages carry the page's branding: Discord and Slack show the page's name and icon, with the status, impact and affected components as fields and maintenance times in each reader's own time zone; emails show the page's logo and a colored status line.
  • A status page can post every incident and update to your organization's notification channels too. Each post picks who hears about it: which subscriber types and which channels, or nobody for a quiet fix.
  • New API endpoints let CI and scripts post and update incidents and maintenance: /api/v1/status-pages/{pageId}/incidents and its updates, with the same choice of who is notified.

Fixed

  • A status page behind a Cloudflare Tunnel now links to its https address.
  • The notification channel API no longer asks for scope, quiet hours and throttle: new channels get the same defaults as in the dashboard, and a change keeps the fields it leaves out.

Polished

  • Unused code and an unused package were removed from the project.

New

  • Status pages: a public page that shows visitors how your services are doing, opened from Status pages in the sidebar.
  • Components follow the uptime checks of the services you pick; visitors see the names you give them, never service names or addresses. Group them under headings and set their order.
  • Incidents and maintenance: report an incident and post updates as you learn more. Plan maintenance with a start and an end. Outages found by uptime checks show up on their own, unless you turn that off.
  • Templates fill in a saved incident message in one click. Postmortems add a longer write-up to a resolved incident.
  • Design with a live preview for desktop and phone: four ready-made looks, logos for light and dark, a favicon, accent color, theme, font, corners, spacing, daily bars for 30, 60 or 90 days, uptime percent, a response time chart, a banner, header links, footer text and custom CSS.
  • Words and language: reword or translate any text on the page, and show dates in a chosen language.
  • Who can see it: public, behind a password, or a draft only your team can open.
  • Own domain, like status.example.com, reached through the server's public IP or a Cloudflare Tunnel, with HTTP or HTTPS and an automatic certificate or one of your own; only the status page answers on that domain.
  • Use it elsewhere: an SVG badge, a website widget, JSON and RSS.
  • A new Status pages permission controls who can manage them. Owners, Admins and Developers have it by default.

Polished

  • The "App unavailable" and "No app here" pages show your branding icon in the browser tab.
  • Unticking a server in Servers & registry saves at once, even when that server is gone; its cleanup runs in the background. Moving an app off a server that no longer answers does not wait for it either.

Fixed

  • The dashboard domain's HTTPS check no longer fails on servers that cannot reach their own public address, which is common with cloud hosts. The check now runs on the server itself: when the request to the domain gets no answer, Serve asks its own proxy directly, under the domain's name and with its certificate checked. If the proxy answers, the step passes and says so. Visitors from outside were never affected.

Fixed

  • The Main server dialog now stays open until the page shows the new main server. Before, it closed as soon as the switch was done, while the page still showed the old main server for a few more seconds, which looked like the switch had not worked.

Fixed

  • Making another server the main one is no longer refused when the app's servers share no private network, since the main server is how visitors leave a failing server and should never be blocked. The dialog now shows a warning instead: the servers outside the private network get no visitors, so every visitor goes to the new main server until they share one again.
  • A server that left the private network after it was added no longer blocks saving the Servers settings. It shows a warning instead, so other changes (like the build server or registry) still save. Adding a new server outside the private network with load balancing on is still refused.

Fixed

  • "Point to" and changing the main server now work for domains whose Cloudflare account was disconnected and then connected again. Such a domain kept its zone but lost the link to the account, so Serve said it could only change the record in a connected Cloudflare account. Serve now finds the connected account that holds the domain's zone, links it again, and changes the record.

New

  • A domain whose DNS points at another server of the app instead of the main one shows "Points to" and that server's name; when the domain's zone is in a connected Cloudflare account, a "Point to" button next to it changes the record to the main server in one click. Only that domain's record changes (never a wildcard record), and its Cloudflare proxy setting stays as it is.
  • In Settings → Servers & registry, a server that shares no private network with the main server now says so on its row. Ticking one with load balancing on shows the problem inside the card, with a link to Private networks, and Save stays off until it is fixed.

Fixed

  • A dashboard tab left open across an update could no longer run actions: a click did nothing, with no error. Each release now has its own deployment ID, so an old tab reloads instead; if an action still hits an old page, it now says that Serve was updated and asks for a reload.

Fixed

  • Load balancing only reaches other servers through a private network; Serve now enforces that instead of silently sending every visitor to the main server. Adding a server that shares no private network with the app's main server is refused while load balancing is on, with a message on how to fix it (turning load balancing off lets the app run there without visitors). Making a server the main one is refused the same way when it cannot reach the other servers. When a server leaves the private network later, the Domains & ports tab shows a warning that every visitor now goes to the main server, with a link to Private networks.

New

  • When the domain's zone is in a connected Cloudflare account, switching the main server now points the domain's A record at the new server too, even when you made the record yourself, as long as it pointed at the old main server; its proxy (orange cloud) setting is kept. Records pointing anywhere else are left alone, and Serve tells you to update them.
  • Force starting a queued deployment now cancels the running deployment of the same service, and any older ones still waiting, then starts at once, instead of refusing while another deployment of the service runs. The cancelled deployment stops, and the previous version keeps running until the new one is live.

Polished

  • The HTTP options on the Domains & ports tab are split into cards: Limits and timeouts, Load balancing, Access control, Headers, Performance and routing, and Advanced, each with its own Apply that changes only its own settings.

Polished

  • Deploys to apps on servers of mixed CPU types are faster. When an app runs on ARM servers next to Intel or AMD ones, Serve now builds one image per CPU type, all at the same time, instead of waiting for the main build to finish first.
  • One server of each other CPU type builds the image at the same time as the main build, with the app's own server going first for its type.
  • Other servers of that same CPU type copy the image from the one that built it, instead of building it again; with two ARM and two AMD servers, there are two builds side by side and the other two only copy.
  • Every build uses the same commit; if the branch moves during the deploy, the deploy stops and asks for a redeploy.
  • If the main build or the app's own server fails, the other builds stop too.
  • Apps deployed from a ready-made image are unchanged: each server still pulls the image for its own CPU type.

New

  • Apps with more than one replica, or running on several servers, can pick how visitors are spread. Find it in Domains & ports → HTTP options → Load balancing.
  • Round robin gives each replica visitors in turn, and is the default.
  • Least busy sends each visitor to the replica with the fewest open requests, good for slow requests like uploads, streams or AI calls.
  • Sticky sessions keeps a visitor on the same replica; this replaces the old Sticky sessions switch, and apps that had it on keep it.
  • Main server first sends visitors only to the main server's replicas; when none of them answers its health check, the other servers take the visitors until the main server is back, within about 10 seconds, showing "Standby" in Settings → Servers while they wait.
  • These strategies work with nginx, Caddy and Traefik.
  • Once you set your own product name or logo in Settings → Branding, the sign-in pages show only your logo and name above the form; the panel about Serve, the greeting and the version number are gone. The product name can be left blank, which shows Serve's name instead.

Polished

  • A domain whose DNS points at another server of the same app now says "Points to" and names that server, instead of a red "Points elsewhere", with a tooltip explaining what to change.
  • After you change an app's main server, the DNS checks run again against the new server.
  • The sidebar header is one row: logo, name with the version under it, and the organization switcher.
  • Settings is in the account menu for instance admins.
  • On the sign-in page, password sign-in comes first and the GitHub, Google and other sign-in buttons are below it.
